messages.author: 91b29aed6400ef48
messages.subject: Rich Club
parts:
Hi Chris,

Would you be able to clarify the following questions about rich club? 

1. I used the rich_core function to calculate the cut-off degree for inclusion in the rich club. The attached figure shows the normalized rich club coefficient vs degree. Should I choose the cut-off value at the start of the shaded rich-core, k=13 or should I choose the cut-off at which there is separation between the two groups, k=19? 

2. I see that the normalized rich club coefficient is only significant for the Super group at a range of degrees. Does that mean the Control group has no rich clubs? Although, I am able to identify rich clubs at k=13 for the Control group. 

3. How do I interpret the normalized rich club coefficients > 1 --- For example a value of 1.1 versus a higher value of 1.5?

4. Lastly, I am able to plot the rich club on a graph but is there a way to list the regions and connections in a data table? 

[I am using both brainGraph and user guide of version 2.0.2]

Thank you in advance for your help,
Jaiashre.

messages.author: dadcb4fd6a01f8d1
messages.subject: Re: [brainGraph-help] Rich Club
parts:
Hi Jaiashre,

1. As Ma & Mondragon (2015) write, there isn't a consensus method for defining the vertices that make up the rich club. So their *rich core* method determines the rich club members without regard to a random graph model or statistical significance. To answer your question, there also isn't a consensus for choosing a cut-off value when considering multiple groups at once. You may decide on the minimum of the group-specific values, or the maximum, or some other number (the plotting function automatically shades in starting at the maximum across groups). Choosing where there is "separation" is too arbitrary, I would think.

2. It is possible that there is statistical significance for both groups; but the asterisks *might* be plotted on top of one another. This would be a bug in the plotting function (I have to double-check). To see the values, you can access the data by something like:
plot_rich_norm(rich.dt, ...)$data

i.e., by accessing the "data" element of the function's return object.

3. Normalized rich-club coefficients that are > 1 are considered to indicate the presence of rich-club ordering in the network. But the value isn't necessarily significant, this requires comparison to a set of random graphs. I don't think you can compare normalized rich-club coefficients between groups (e.g., 1.1 vs. 1.5). The values are only meaningful relative to the set of random graphs, and therefore the topology of the observed network.

4. Sure, if you use "rich_core" you can do something like:

core <- rich_core(g)
vertex_attr_dt(g)[degree > core$k.r]

If you otherwise create "rich.dt" (following the User Guide), you can just do:
rich.dt[p < .05]

Or change to "p.fdr", or change the ".05" to ".01", etc.

Chris

messages.author: dadcb4fd6a01f8d1
messages.subject: Re: [brainGraph-help] Rich Club
parts:
You can simply calculate the between-group difference in (non-normalized) rich-club coefficients, and similarly do so for the randomized networks; i.e., get the differences in "phi.norm" for the 1,000 (or however many) random networks that were generated. See e.g. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3915050/

Chris

Here is the code I used to plot that figure:

plot_brainGraph_multi(g, groups=1:2, N=N,filename='Figure02_richClub_revision.png',
  subgraph=list(paste('degree >=', rich_core(g[[1]][[N]])$k.r),
                       paste('degree >=', rich_core(g[[2]][[N]])$k.r)),
  vertex.color='color.lobe', edge.color='color.lobe', vertex.size='degree',
  vertex.label=NA, sub=NULL, cex.main=4)

As you can see, I used "rich_core" to decide which vertices to include (via the "subgraph") argument.

If you would like to change the edge attribute "size.rich", you would have to do something like the following (this is actually the code from the function "rich_club_attrs"):
E(g)[E(g)$type.rich == 'rich-club']$size.rich <- 3.5
E(g)[E(g)$type.rich == 'feeder']$size.rich <- 1.5
E(g)[E(g)$type.rich == 'local']$size.rich <- 0.5

For the *vertex* attribute "size.rich", here is from the same function:
V(g)[V(g)$rich == 1]$size.rich <- vec.transform(V(g)[which(V(g)$rich == 1)]$degree, 3, 15

What "vec.transform" does is it takes a numeric input vector (in this case, the degree sequence of the rich-club vertices), and "transforms" it so that it fits into a range of 3 to 15. So change these values to something else, or simply do something like:

V(g)[V(g)$rich == 1]$size.rich <- 10
V(g)[V(g)$rich == 0]$size.rich <- 1

or whatever you like.

Chris

On Tuesday, June 12, 2018 at 2:54:50 PM UTC-5, Chris Watson wrote:
Hi Jaiashre,

1. As Ma & Mondragon (2015) write, there isn't a consensus method for defining the vertices that make up the rich club. So their *rich core* method determines the rich club members without regard to a random graph model or statistical significance. To answer your question, there also isn't a consensus for choosing a cut-off value when considering multiple groups at once. You may decide on the minimum of the group-specific values, or the maximum, or some other number (the plotting function automatically shades in starting at the maximum across groups). Choosing where there is "separation" is too arbitrary, I would think.

2. It is possible that there is statistical significance for both groups; but the asterisks *might* be plotted on top of one another. This would be a bug in the plotting function (I have to double-check). To see the values, you can access the data by something like:
plot_rich_norm(rich.dt, ...)$data

i.e., by accessing the "data" element of the function's return object.

3. Normalized rich-club coefficients that are > 1 are considered to indicate the presence of rich-club ordering in the network. But the value isn't necessarily significant, this requires comparison to a set of random graphs. I don't think you can compare normalized rich-club coefficients between groups (e.g., 1.1 vs. 1.5). The values are only meaningful relative to the set of random graphs, and therefore the topology of the observed network.

4. Sure, if you use "rich_core" you can do something like:

core <- rich_core(g)
vertex_attr_dt(g)[degree > core$k.r]

If you otherwise create "rich.dt" (following the User Guide), you can just do:
rich.dt[p < .05]

Or change to "p.fdr", or change the ".05" to ".01", etc.

Chris
